summary: For ages 7–9, teach what a tsunami is and why it behaves so counter-intuitively: a sudden movement of the sea floor (undersea earthquake or volcanic eruption, also landslides) pushes the whole column of water, creating a low wave that races across the open ocean very fast and can reach distant coasts, then slows, stacks up tall and floods when it reaches shallow coast. Emphasise the safety-empowering natural warning signs: the sea sometimes drawing far back first (this does not always happen), and strong shaking near the coast. Contrast the whole-depth tsunami with an ordinary surface wind wave. Keep the tone matter-of-fact and reassuring (warning systems now exist), not frightening. In England this sits in KS2 Geography (physical geography hazards), not KS2 science.
misconceptions: A tsunami is one giant tall breaking/surfing wave (in deep water it is low; it grows and floods at the coast, often as a fast surge, sometimes a series of waves).
Tsunamis are caused by wind or storms (they are caused by sudden sea-floor movement — undersea earthquakes or eruptions, also landslides).
There is only one wave (tsunamis often arrive as several waves; later ones can be larger).
It's safe once the first wave passes / when the sea pulls back it's a chance to explore (the draw-back is a warning to flee; more water is coming).
Tsunamis are the same as ordinary tides (unrelated to daily tides; 'tidal wave' is a misleading old name).

activities.title: Set off the wave: watch it grow at the shore
steps: Use a side-view cross-section of the ocean (deep water on one side, a shelving beach on the other) and trigger an undersea earthquake or eruption that moves the sea floor.

Watch the wave leave low and almost flat, racing across the deep ocean very fast; note a speed readout showing how quickly it crosses, and that it can spread right across the open ocean to reach distant coasts.
Watch what happens as the water gets shallow near the coast: the wave slows, stacks up and towers, then floods inland.
Predict out loud before triggering: 'Will the wave be tall out in the deep ocean, or will it grow near the shore?' Then check.
Describe the whole causal chain in your own words: sea floor moves → whole water column pushed → fast low wave spreads across the ocean → grows tall and floods at the shallow coast.
activities.insight: A tsunami is not a single tall surfing wave; it is the whole depth of water being pushed, staying low and fast as it spreads across deep ocean and only rearing up and flooding where the water becomes shallow at the coast.

activities.title: The sea pulls back: a warning to run
steps: Watch the shoreline just before the surge arrives: in this example the water races OUT, exposing the sea bed, before flooding back in (this often happens, but not with every tsunami).
Answer: 'If you were at the beach and the sea suddenly pulled far back, exposing the sand, what would that mean and what would you do?'
Learn and repeat the safety rule: sea pulling back = get to high ground quickly; do not walk out onto the newly exposed sand.
Note that a tsunami can arrive as several waves, and later ones can be larger — it is not safe once the first wave passes.
activities.insight: A receding shoreline is a natural warning sign of an approaching tsunami; the correct, empowering response is to move immediately to high ground, not to explore the exposed sea bed. The sea does not always pull back first, so strong shaking near the coast or an official warning also means go to high ground.

activities.title: Wind wave vs whole-depth tsunami
steps: Compare a small wind-blown wave with a tsunami using a side-by-side toggle: the wind wave is a surface movement; the tsunami moves the whole depth of the water.
Explain in your own words how a tsunami is different from an ordinary wave at the beach.
Connect the difference to energy: because a tsunami moves the whole water column, it carries vastly more water and energy than a surface wave.
Identify the real cause of each: wind for ordinary waves, sudden sea-floor movement for a tsunami (and note a tsunami is unrelated to daily tides — 'tidal wave' is a misleading old name).
activities.insight: A tsunami differs fundamentally from a wind wave: wind waves are surface movements, while a tsunami moves the entire depth of the ocean and therefore carries far more water and energy.

activities.title: Make it real: a told account and warning systems
steps: Hear or read a brief, age-appropriate account of a real tsunami to understand that this really happens, without dwelling on distressing detail.
Discuss what people now do to stay safe: warning systems exist, and the natural signs (the sea drawing back, strong shaking near the coast) can give time to move.
Retell the causal chain and the safety rule to a partner or adult as if explaining it to someone who has never heard of a tsunami.
activities.insight: Tsunamis are real natural hazards, but people are not helpless: understanding the cause, recognising warning signs, and warning systems all help keep people safe.

checkQuestion: Lots of people picture a tsunami as one giant curling wave, like a huge version of a surfing wave, appearing out of nowhere at the beach. Is that what a tsunami is really like? What causes it, and what might you notice at the shore just before it arrives?
checkAnswer: Not quite — a tsunami isn't a single curling surf wave. It's caused by a sudden movement of the sea floor (an undersea earthquake or eruption) that pushes the whole column of water. It races across the ocean very fast, low in deep water, then piles up high at the coast as a fast-rising surge or series of waves. A warning sign is the sea DRAWING BACK, exposing the sea bed, just before it arrives.
